title: CDNs
objective: See how serving files from servers near users cuts their wait and takes load off the origin.
simplifies: Three groups of users at illustrative distances (20, 80 and 200 ms round trips); an edge answers every cacheable request (as if always warm); the origin handles 4 requests at a time. Real CDNs miss sometimes, need cache rules (headers like Cache-Control), and cost money per gigabyte.

challenges.title: Far-away users
challenges.prompt: Keep the typical wait for far users at 100 ms or less for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: Far users are 200 ms away (round trip). Without a CDN, roughly how long is their typical wait for a file?

options.explanation: Right. The request and the connection both cross the distance: the round trips add up.
That is the near users' distance.
Distance always costs time; signals don't travel instantly.

challenges.hint: You can't move the users closer. Can you move copies of the files closer to them?
challenges.explain: With CDN edges, cacheable files are answered from a server near each group of users, so far users stop paying for the long trip.

challenges.title: Origin overload
challenges.prompt: Traffic is 150 requests a second and the CDN is on, but little is cacheable. Keep errors at 1% or less for 10 seconds.
challenges.hint: Everything the edges can't answer still goes to the origin. How could more of it be answered at the edge?
challenges.explain: Making more responses cacheable (static files, sensible cache rules) means the edges answer them, and the origin only sees what truly has to come from it.

quiz.prompt: What does a CDN mostly speed up?

options.text: Files that can be cached, for users far from the origin
options.explanation: Right. Copies near users cut the distance; dynamic, per-user answers still come from the origin.
Writes still go to the origin.
Only what an edge can answer from a copy.

quiz.prompt: Besides speed, what else does a CDN give the origin?

options.text: Less traffic, because edges answer cacheable requests
options.explanation: Right. The origin then only handles what can't be cached.
Edges absorb traffic; they don't add to it.
Taking load off the origin is a big part of the point.
